cons: Generative features blur the academic integrity line without an explicit policy
Admin analytics carry FERPA handling requirements
Free consumer installs can coexist with the campus licence and bypass controls
name: Grammarly for Education
pros: Meaningful help at scale for non-native English writers
Admin oversight not available on consumer tier
files: Text in place, in browsers and editors.
value: Writing assistance deployed at institutional scale across students and staff, with campus admin controls and reporting. The product itself is the same as the business edition; the conversation around it is not.
engine: Same as Grammarly. Proprietary models, some generative features on third-party models.
tagline: The campus licence of Grammarly, and the centre of the academic integrity debate.
use_cases: Improving student writing clarity and mechanics at scale
Identifying writing patterns across the student body through admin analytics
Non-native English speakers developing academic writing competence
integrations: Learning management system connectors on some tiers
governance_note: The governance question in education is not the product, it is the policy. Grammarly corrects grammar; the moment its generative features write sentences, the academic integrity question is live. Institutions need a clear published policy on which features are within-bounds and which are not, before deploying a campus licence rather than after the first academic misconduct case. The admin analytics also surface usage patterns that have FERPA implications if the data is not handled as an education record.
training_optout: Institutional terms address data use. Confirm which terms apply to the specific agreement, not the product marketing.
